newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia May D&B credit rating stable at DB3a.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia May D&B credit rating stable at DB3a.

text.p: Slovenia's overall risk profile remained "broadly favourable" as the government maintained a firm hand on the economy, credit agency Dun and Bradstreet's (D&B) Ljubljana representative said on Tuesday.
The agency kept its rating for Slovenia at DB3a for May, unchanged for 11 consecutive months, placing it second in the region just behind the Czech Republic and ahead of Poland.

The agency expressed concern about an increase in energy prices and the possibility of a rise in wage pressures amid the lack of a new collective agreement on labour benefits. The current agreement is due to expire at the end of May.

In April, year-on-year consumer prices rose 8.2 percent from a year ago, up from 7.4 percent in March and down from 10.7 percent in the same month a year ago. Monthly average gross wages rose 14.1 percent to 136,811 tolars ($885) in February from a year earlier.

"While the 1996 fiscal year budget is estimated to have shown near-balance, revenues and expenditures each equated to a large 45.9 percent of GDP with little scope for cutting expenditure, especially given that Desus' presence in the coalition will mean maintained prensions payments," D&B said.
Following last November's general elections, Slovenia is governed by a coalition of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, the conservative People's Party and the pensioners' party Desus.
The agency also warned that reluctance to grant foreigners easy access to Slovenia's capital markets was likely to put a dampener on international investor interest.

"There has been some fresh investor interest, but central bank regulations forcing international investors to open custody share trading accounts at 14 licensed banks are set to deter short and medium term portfolio inflows," the agency said.

Since the central bank announced its move in February, the blue-chip SBI index has lost more than 20 percent, while average daily trading volumes on the bourse shrunk to a mere third of their previous level. -- Novica Mihajlovic, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
